data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["In physical component failure (e.g., generators), wear-and-tear is often well-modeled by independent Weibull distributions; in software systems, common-mode failures (bugs) and common-cause failures (administrative errors, dependency outages) dominate the tail risk, violating independence assumptions.","Physical redundancy often assumes identical components for ease of maintenance; organizational/technical diversity in decentralized systems introduces its own operational complexities and integration failure modes."],"overturn_conditions":["Discovery of a latent variable that renders the independence conditional, demonstrating that observed decorrelation was merely a sampling artifact of a limited observation window.","A formal proof that the monolith's internal redundancy mechanisms are isomorphic to the decentralized independence mechanisms, reducing the architectural distinction to an implementation detail."],"shared_structure":["Probabilistic dependence structure under latent variables (Pearl's Causal Bayesian Networks).","The distinction between marginal independence and conditional independence given a common cause (Y \u22a5\u22a5 X, but Y /\u22a5\u22a5 X | Z).","System resilience is an emergent property of the joint probability distribution of component failures, not merely a count of redundant components."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001","SRC_002"],"transfer_claims":["The statistical distinction between observing P(X,Y) \u2248 P(X)P(Y) and the causal mechanism that generates this independence is paramount.","Just as 'spurious correlation' in statistics requires a causal intervention to distinguish from genuine dependence, 'observed independence' in distributed systems requires a demonstration of causal independence to be predictive of future resilience under novel shared stresses.","Therefore, the number of services (N) is a red herring; the critical variable is the diversity of their causal graphs."]},"claim":"Decentralized small-service networks are more resilient than a single highly-redundant monolith only when an empirically demonstrable causal independence barrier exists\u2014typically a separation of supply chains, codebases, operational teams, and regulatory jurisdictions. Without such a mechanism, observed decorrelation is epistemically fragile and likely to collapse under shared-cause discovery.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a shared dependency (e.g., a common DNS provider, a ubiquitous cryptographic library, or a shared cloud region outage) is found to cause simultaneous failures, the decentralized network's presumed independence is falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the monolith implements active redundancy with diverse code implementations (N-version programming) and diverse physical infrastructure, it may achieve comparable or superior independence.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the decentralized services share the same operational staff or supply chain, their independence is illusory and they inherit correlated failure modes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Resilience to correlated failure is fundamentally about the conditional probability P(fail_i | fail_j, C) under some shared latent cause C. A monolith with internal redundancy can eliminate single points of failure at the component level (N+1, N+2), but its CDF collapses if C triggers a shared bug, resource exhaustion, or administrative error. Decentralized services CAN achieve lower P(fail_i | fail_j) IF and only IF they possess distinct causal graphs for their C-events (different teams, codebases, cloud providers, failure modes). This independence is not intrinsic to 'decentralization' but is a constructed property achieved through specific engineering and organizational mechanisms.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
